summary: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy — not auscultation — is the gold standard for confirming lung isolation device position, since clinical exam alone has been shown to miss malposition in a substantial fraction of cases, and hypoxemia troubleshooting follows a logical sequence: check position first, suction, then escalate FiO2/CPAP rather than jumping straight to increasing oxygen.
whyThisMatters: A malpositioned double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker is common enough, and consequential enough for oxygenation, that clinical exam alone is genuinely inadequate for confirming placement — this is one of those areas where the 'obvious' bedside check (listening for breath sounds) has been directly shown to underperform a specific alternative (bronchoscopy), which is worth knowing explicitly rather than assuming auscultation is good enough.
clinicalTakeaway:
Confirm double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker position with fiberoptic bronchoscopy, not clinical exam alone — malposition by clinical assessment alone has been reported in as many as half of cases in some series.

Position can shift during the case from surgical manipulation or patient repositioning — if hypoxemia develops intraoperatively, re-confirm position with a repeat bronchoscopic look rather than assuming your initial placement is still correct.

When hypoxemia occurs:
1. Check/correct tube position FIRST.
2. Then suction secretions from both lumens.
3. THEN escalate — increase FiO2, apply CPAP to the non-ventilated lung, or use lung recruitment maneuvers on the ventilated lung.

Rather than jumping straight to increasing FiO2 without checking position first.

rows: A tube with two separate lumens, one extending into a mainstem bronchus (isolating that lung) and one ending in the trachea (ventilating the other lung)
Allows fully independent lung isolation AND independent suctioning/CPAP application to either lung — the more versatile option for most routine thoracic cases
A balloon-tipped catheter passed through (or alongside) a standard single-lumen ETT and advanced into the target mainstem bronchus to occlude it

Often easier to place in a difficult airway, a patient with an existing tracheostomy, or when postoperative ventilation with a standard single-lumen tube is anticipated — but doesn't allow the same independent suctioning/CPAP flexibility on the blocked side, and can be more prone to displacement during surgical manipulation

body.text: Confirming position — bronchoscopy, not just auscultation

Clinical exam (auscultation, chest rise, end-tidal CO2 waveform) alone is NOT reliable enough to confirm lung isolation device position — reported malposition rates by clinical assessment alone run as high as roughly 50% in some series. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy through the tube is the gold-standard confirmation method and should be used, not skipped in favor of auscultation alone.

items: Confirm position immediately after placement AND after any subsequent patient repositioning (e.g. moving into lateral decubitus) — position that looked correct supine can shift once the patient is repositioned for the case.

Position can also shift DURING the case from surgical manipulation of the lung/mediastinum — if unexplained hypoxemia develops intraoperatively, re-confirm position with a repeat bronchoscopic look rather than assuming the initial placement is still correct.

body.text: Hypoxemia during one-lung ventilation — the troubleshooting sequence

items: 1. CHECK/CORRECT TUBE POSITION FIRST via bronchoscopy — this is the most common correctable cause and should be checked before escalating anything else.
2. SUCTION secretions from both lumens/the ventilated lung — retained secretions are a common, easily correctable contributor.

3. Only after position and secretions are addressed: escalate — increase FiO2 (often to 1.0), apply CPAP to the NON-ventilated lung (this provides some passive oxygenation to that lung without meaningfully interfering with the surgical field in most cases), or use a lung recruitment maneuver on the VENTILATED lung if atelectasis is contributing.

Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in the non-ventilated lung is actually a helpful, protective physiologic response here — it redirects blood flow away from the non-ventilated (unoxygenated) lung toward the ventilated one, improving the ventilation-perfusion match. Worth knowing that volatile anesthetic agents can blunt this response at higher concentrations, which is a factor to consider (alongside other considerations) if hypoxemia persists despite the above steps.

If hypoxemia remains refractory despite this sequence, consider intermittent two-lung ventilation (with surgeon coordination) as a temporizing measure while further troubleshooting or reassessing the surgical plan.
